course.title: Solar Energy
course.description: How sunlight becomes electricity, from the physics of the solar cell to the design of a working photovoltaic system, with worked numbers at every step. Structure adapted from TU Delft OpenCourseWare (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0); all explanations original.

questions.prompt: The power of sunlight reaching a surface, measured in W/m^2, is called...
questions.explanation: Irradiance is power per unit area; the energy that accumulates over time is called irradiation. See 'The solar resource'.

questions.prompt: In a semiconductor, the minimum photon energy needed to free an electron for conduction is set by the...
questions.explanation: Only photons with energy at or above the band gap can lift an electron across it. See 'Semiconductor basics'.

questions.prompt: The direct conversion of light into an electrical voltage inside a material is known as the...
questions.explanation: The photovoltaic effect is generation of a voltage from absorbed light, the basis of every solar cell.

questions.prompt: The power of a solar cell equals...
questions.explanation: Electrical power is P = V*I; a solar cell is operated where this product is largest.

questions.prompt: Under standard test conditions the reference irradiance used to rate solar modules is...
questions.explanation: Standard test conditions use 1000 W/m^2, a cell temperature of 25 degrees C, and the AM1.5 spectrum.

questions.prompt: Connecting solar cells in series mainly increases the...
questions.explanation: Series connection adds voltages; parallel connection adds currents. See 'From cell to module to array'.

questions.prompt: As a silicon module gets hotter, its output power usually...
questions.explanation: Silicon has a negative temperature coefficient, so power drops as temperature rises above 25 degrees C.

questions.prompt: A device that converts the direct current from panels into alternating current for the grid is a(n)...
questions.explanation: The inverter turns DC into AC and is a core part of the balance of system.

lessons.title: The solar resource: Sun, spectrum, irradiance, air mass
lessons.grammar_note: Keep irradiance (power now, in W/m^2) separate from irradiation (energy over time, in kWh/m^2) - mixing them up is the most common unit slip in this course.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe where the Sun's energy comes from, read the solar spectrum, and use irradiance and air mass to say how much power a surface receives. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what are the units of irradiance, and what does the word measure?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The Sun radiates roughly like a hot body at about 5800 K, so its light spreads across the spectrum with most energy in the visible range and a long tail into the infrared. Just outside the atmosphere the incoming power is about 1361 W/m^2, the solar constant. As sunlight travels down through the atmosphere, gases scatter and absorb part of it, so a clear noon at sea level delivers close to 1000 W/m^2. How much atmosphere the light crosses is captured by the air mass, AM = 1 / cos(z), where z is the angle of the Sun from straight overhead. Directly overhead gives AM1, and the industry reference spectrum, AM1.5, corresponds to the Sun about 48 degrees from vertical, a fair stand-in for typical mid-latitude conditions.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Air mass: if the Sun sits 60 degrees from overhead, cos(60) = 0.5, so AM = 1 / 0.5 = 2 - the light crosses twice the straight-down thickness of atmosphere. Irradiation from irradiance: a rooftop receives an average 500 W/m^2 over 6 hours of useful sun. Energy per square metre is 500 W/m^2 * 6 h = 3000 Wh/m^2 = 3.0 kWh/m^2 for the day. Peak sun hours: that same 3.0 kWh/m^2 is often quoted as 3.0 peak sun hours, meaning 3 hours at the reference 1000 W/m^2 would deliver the same energy.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) The Sun is 30 degrees from overhead; find the air mass (cos(30) is about 0.87). 2) A panel plane averages 700 W/m^2 for 5 hours; how much energy in kWh/m^2? 3) A site gets 4.5 kWh/m^2 per day; how many peak sun hours is that? 4) Which carries more energy, a blue photon or a red photon? 5) Is 1361 W/m^2 measured above or below the atmosphere? Answers: 1) AM = 1 / 0.87 = about 1.15. 2) 700 * 5 = 3500 Wh/m^2 = 3.5 kWh/m^2. 3) 4.5 peak sun hours. 4) The blue photon, because shorter wavelength means higher energy. 5) Above the atmosphere; at the surface a clear noon is closer to 1000 W/m^2.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reporting irradiance in kWh, which is an energy unit, not power. Mistake: assuming air mass is always 1 - it grows as the Sun drops toward the horizon. Exit: (a) What is the air mass when the Sun is straight overhead? (b) A surface sees 1000 W/m^2 for 2 hours; how much energy per square metre? Answers: AM1; 2.0 kWh/m^2.

lessons.title: Semiconductor basics: band gap, doping, p-n junction
lessons.grammar_note: A handy conversion: a photon's energy in electron-volts is about 1240 divided by its wavelength in nanometres, so E(eV) = 1240 / lambda(nm).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what a band gap is, tell n-type from p-type material, and describe the electric field that forms at a p-n junction. Warm-up: which sets the smallest photon energy a cell can use, the band gap or the air mass?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: In a semiconductor the electrons that could carry current sit in a filled valence band, separated from an empty conduction band by an energy gap called the band gap, Eg. Crystalline silicon has Eg of about 1.12 eV. A photon can lift an electron across the gap only if its energy is at least Eg; lower-energy photons pass through unused, and any energy a photon carries above Eg is quickly lost as heat. Pure silicon conducts poorly, so we dope it: adding a little phosphorus donates spare electrons and makes n-type material, while adding a little boron creates electron vacancies, called holes, and makes p-type material. Join an n-type layer to a p-type layer and electrons and holes diffuse across the boundary, leaving behind fixed charges that build a permanent internal electric field. That field-filled boundary is the p-n junction, the engine at the heart of a solar cell.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Photon energy from wavelength: green light near 550 nm carries E = 1240 / 550 = about 2.25 eV, well above silicon's 1.12 eV, so it is easily absorbed. Cutoff wavelength: the longest wavelength silicon can use satisfies 1.12 = 1240 / lambda, so lambda = 1240 / 1.12 = about 1107 nm - light beyond roughly 1100 nm in the near infrared slips through unabsorbed. Thermalization: a 2.25 eV photon that only needed 1.12 eV wastes about 2.25 - 1.12 = 1.13 eV as heat, one reason a single-junction cell cannot reach 100%.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Find the energy of a 620 nm red photon in eV. 2) Can a 1500 nm infrared photon free an electron in silicon (Eg = 1.12 eV)? 3) Does adding phosphorus make n-type or p-type silicon? 4) What mobile particle does p-type doping add? 5) What forms at the boundary of a p-n junction? Answers: 1) 1240 / 620 = 2.0 eV. 2) Its energy is 1240 / 1500 = about 0.83 eV, below 1.12 eV, so no. 3) n-type, because phosphorus donates electrons. 4) Holes, the mobile vacancies that act as positive carriers. 5) A depletion region with a built-in electric field.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking a brighter light can push a below-gap photon across the gap - it is each photon's energy that matters, not the intensity. Mistake: swapping n-type and p-type dopants. Exit: (a) What is silicon's band gap in eV? (b) Which dopant makes p-type silicon, boron or phosphorus? Answers: about 1.12 eV; boron.

lessons.title: How a solar cell works: the photovoltaic effect
lessons.grammar_note: Generation is the useful step (light makes a free electron-hole pair); recombination is the loss (a pair disappears before it can be collected). A good cell maximises the first and minimises the second.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Trace the path from an absorbed photon to a current in a wire, and name the loss that competes with it. Warm-up: what is the name for a material's direct conversion of light into a voltage?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: When a photon with energy at or above the band gap is absorbed, it lifts an electron into the conduction band and leaves a hole behind - this is generation of an electron-hole pair. Near the p-n junction the built-in electric field sweeps the freed electron toward the n-side and the hole toward the p-side, separating the charges before they can fall back together. Connect the two sides through an external wire and the collected electrons flow around the circuit, delivering current at a voltage: that is the photovoltaic effect. The competing process is recombination, where an electron and hole meet and release their energy as heat or light instead of reaching the contacts. Every recombination event is a lost charge, so cell design is a constant fight to collect carriers before they recombine.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Counting current from photons: suppose 5 * 10^18 useful photons strike a cell each second and 90% generate a collected electron. That is 4.5 * 10^18 electrons per second. Multiplying by the electron charge 1.6 * 10^-19 C gives a current of 4.5 * 10^18 * 1.6 * 10^-19 = about 0.72 A. Effect of recombination: if instead only 70% of pairs are collected, the current falls to 5 * 10^18 * 0.70 * 1.6 * 10^-19 = 0.56 A, a direct loss of output. Voltage limit: the usable voltage of a silicon cell is a fraction of its 1.12 eV gap, typically about 0.6 to 0.7 V, because some energy is always given up to separate and collect the carriers.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In one word, what makes a free electron-hole pair? 2) In one word, what is the loss process that destroys a pair? 3) Which way does the junction field push the freed electron, toward the n-side or the p-side? 4) If 2 * 10^18 electrons per second are collected, what current is that (charge = 1.6 * 10^-19 C)? 5) Roughly what open-circuit voltage does a single silicon cell reach? Answers: 1) Generation. 2) Recombination. 3) Toward the n-side. 4) 2 * 10^18 * 1.6 * 10^-19 = 0.32 A. 5) About 0.6 to 0.7 V.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: expecting one photon to free many electrons - in a standard cell each absorbed photon frees at most one pair. Mistake: thinking a silicon cell's voltage equals its 1.12 eV gap; it is always noticeably less. Exit: (a) Which process do you want to maximise, generation or recombination? (b) What effect turns absorbed light into a voltage? Answers: generation; the photovoltaic effect.

questions.prompt: Directly overhead, the Sun corresponds to an air mass of...
questions.explanation: AM = 1 / cos(0) = 1; AM1.5 is the reference spectrum with the Sun about 48 degrees from vertical.

questions.prompt: A surface receives 800 W/m^2 for 5 hours. The energy collected per square metre is...
A photon can free an electron in silicon only if its energy is...
options: at or above the band gap
questions.explanation: The photon must supply at least Eg (about 1.12 eV for silicon) to lift an electron across the gap.

questions.prompt: Adding boron to silicon produces...
questions.explanation: Boron creates holes, making p-type material; phosphorus would make n-type.

questions.prompt: The process that turns absorbed light directly into a voltage is called...
questions.explanation: The photovoltaic effect generates a voltage from absorbed photons at the p-n junction.

questions.prompt: A 1240 nm infrared photon carries about 1.0 eV. For silicon (Eg = 1.12 eV) it is...
options: too weak to free an electron
questions.explanation: 1.0 eV is below the 1.12 eV gap, so the photon passes through unused.

lessons.title: The I-V curve: fill factor, efficiency, maximum power point
lessons.grammar_note: Power is the product P = V*I. On the I-V curve, power is zero at both ends (short circuit has no voltage, open circuit has no current) and largest somewhere in between - that peak is the maximum power point.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Read a cell's current-voltage curve, find its maximum power point, and compute fill factor and efficiency. Warm-up: at open circuit the current is zero and at short circuit the voltage is zero, so what is the electrical power at each of those two endpoints?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Sweep the voltage across a lit cell and plot the current, and you get the I-V curve. Two endpoints anchor it: the short-circuit current Isc, the current when the terminals are shorted (V = 0), and the open-circuit voltage Voc, the voltage with no current drawn (I = 0). Power P = V*I is zero at both ends and reaches a peak in between at the maximum power point, with coordinates Vmp and Imp, so Pmax = Vmp*Imp. The fill factor measures how square the curve is: FF = Pmax / (Voc*Isc) = (Vmp*Imp) / (Voc*Isc), and good silicon cells reach about 0.75 to 0.82. Efficiency is the fraction of incoming light power converted to electricity, eta = Pmax / (irradiance * area), and it can also be written eta = (Voc * Isc * FF) / (irradiance * area).

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Fill factor: a cell has Voc = 0.62 V, Isc = 9.0 A, and at its peak Vmp = 0.52 V, Imp = 8.4 A. Then Pmax = 0.52 * 8.4 = about 4.37 W, and FF = 4.37 / (0.62 * 9.0) = 4.37 / 5.58 = about 0.78. Efficiency: that cell has an area of 0.0243 m^2 and is tested at 1000 W/m^2, so the incoming power is 1000 * 0.0243 = 24.3 W. Then eta = 4.37 / 24.3 = 0.18 = 18%. Check via the second formula: (0.62 * 9.0 * 0.78) / 24.3 = 4.35 / 24.3 = about 0.18, the same 18%.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) A cell has Voc = 0.60 V, Isc = 8.0 A, FF = 0.80; find Pmax. 2) At the maximum power point Vmp = 0.50 V and Imp = 8.0 A; what is Pmax? 3) A 0.02 m^2 cell makes 3.6 W at 1000 W/m^2; find its efficiency. 4) What is the power at the open-circuit point? 5) If Voc*Isc = 5.0 W and Pmax = 4.0 W, what is the fill factor? Answers: 1) Pmax = 0.60 * 8.0 * 0.80 = 3.84 W. 2) 0.50 * 8.0 = 4.0 W. 3) 3.6 / (1000 * 0.02) = 3.6 / 20 = 0.18 = 18%. 4) Zero, because the current is zero there. 5) FF = 4.0 / 5.0 = 0.80.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: multiplying Voc by Isc and calling it the cell's power - that product is always larger than the real Pmax, and the fill factor is exactly the ratio between them. Mistake: forgetting to multiply irradiance by area to get the incoming watts before dividing. Exit: (a) Write the fill factor as a formula. (b) A cell makes 4.0 W from 20 W of incoming light; what is its efficiency? Answers: FF = Pmax / (Voc*Isc); 4.0 / 20 = 20%.

lessons.title: Cell types: crystalline silicon and thin film
lessons.grammar_note: Crystalline silicon wafers are thick, around 180 micrometres; thin-film layers are a hundred times thinner, around 1 to 2 micrometres - the trade is less material against usually lower efficiency.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Tell the main cell families apart and explain the trade-off between efficiency and material use. Warm-up: which material dominates today's solar market, and why might you still choose a thinner alternative?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Most modules sold today use crystalline silicon. Monocrystalline cells are cut from a single silicon crystal, look uniformly dark, and reach commercial efficiencies of roughly 19 to 22%. Multicrystalline (also called polycrystalline) cells are cast from many crystal grains, show a speckled blue pattern, cost a little less, and run a couple of points lower in efficiency. Both use wafers about 180 micrometres thick. Thin-film cells take a different route, depositing a very thin light-absorbing layer such as amorphous silicon, cadmium telluride, or copper indium gallium selenide onto glass or a flexible backing. Thin films use far less material and perform relatively better in heat and diffuse light, but their efficiencies are usually lower, around 10 to 16%, so they need more area for the same power.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Area for a target power: to reach 300 W at 1000 W/m^2 you need an active area of power divided by (irradiance times efficiency). With a 20% crystalline cell that is 300 / (1000 * 0.20) = 1.5 m^2. With a 12% thin-film cell it is 300 / (1000 * 0.12) = 2.5 m^2 - about 67% more area for the same 300 W. Material intuition: dropping wafer thickness from 180 to 1.5 micrometres cuts absorber material per unit area by roughly a factor of 120, which is why thin films can be cheaper per unit area even when they are less efficient.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which is generally more efficient, monocrystalline silicon or amorphous-silicon thin film? 2) How much active area does a 15%-efficient cell need for 300 W at 1000 W/m^2? 3) Name one absorber used in thin-film cells. 4) Roughly how thick is a standard silicon wafer? 5) Give one advantage thin film has over crystalline silicon. Answers: 1) Monocrystalline silicon. 2) 300 / (1000 * 0.15) = 2.0 m^2. 3) Cadmium telluride (or amorphous silicon, or CIGS). 4) About 180 micrometres. 5) Less material used, and often a smaller drop in output when hot or under diffuse light.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming the highest-efficiency cell is always the best choice - when roof area is cheap and budget is tight, a lower-efficiency, lower-cost option can win. Mistake: confusing multicrystalline (many grains) with thin film (a deposited layer). Exit: (a) Which family needs more area per watt, high-efficiency crystalline or lower-efficiency thin film? (b) What is the approximate efficiency range of commercial monocrystalline cells? Answers: thin film; roughly 19 to 22%.

lessons.title: From cell to module to array
lessons.grammar_note: Series adds voltage, parallel adds current. A useful check: total power is unchanged by how you wire identical cells - series or parallel, you get the same watts, just at different volts and amps.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Scale up from a single cell to a module to a full array, and predict the voltage and current of each. Warm-up: connecting cells in series adds up which quantity, voltage or current?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A single silicon cell only makes about 0.6 V, far too little to be useful, so cells are wired in series inside a module. Put 60 cells in series and their voltages add while the current stays that of one cell, giving a module open-circuit voltage of roughly 60 * 0.6 = 36 V. Modules in turn are combined into arrays: wiring modules in series forms a string whose voltages add, while wiring strings in parallel adds their currents. To choose the layout you match the array's voltage and current to what the inverter accepts. Bypass diodes are built across groups of cells so that if part of a module is shaded, current can detour around the weak cells instead of being throttled by them.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Module voltage: 72 cells in series at 0.60 V each give about 72 * 0.60 = 43 V open circuit. String voltage: five 40 V modules in series make a string of 5 * 40 = 200 V, at the current of a single module. Array current: if each string carries 9 A and you connect four strings in parallel, the array delivers 4 * 9 = 36 A at that same 200 V. Array power: 200 V * 36 A = 7200 W = 7.2 kW. Same power, different wiring: ten identical 300 W modules always total 3000 W whether wired as one series string or two parallel strings; only the volts and amps change.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Sixty cells at 0.6 V in series give what module voltage? 2) Four 38 V modules in series make what string voltage? 3) Three parallel strings each at 8 A deliver what total current? 4) A string is 180 V at 8 A; what is its power? 5) To raise voltage without raising current, do you wire in series or parallel? Answers: 1) 60 * 0.6 = 36 V. 2) 4 * 38 = 152 V. 3) 3 * 8 = 24 A. 4) 180 * 8 = 1440 W. 5) In series.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: adding currents for a series connection or adding voltages for a parallel one - it is the other way around. Mistake: forgetting bypass diodes, which keep one shaded cell from dragging down a whole module. Exit: (a) Series connection adds which quantity? (b) A string of six 40 V modules has what open-circuit voltage? Answers: voltage; 6 * 40 = 240 V.

questions.prompt: A cell has Voc = 0.60 V, Isc = 8.0 A, and FF = 0.80. Its maximum power is...
A 0.02 m^2 cell produces 3.6 W under 1000 W/m^2. Its efficiency is...
The fill factor is defined as...
questions.explanation: FF = Pmax / (Voc*Isc); it measures how square the I-V curve is.

questions.prompt: Sixty silicon cells wired in series, each about 0.6 V, give a module voltage near...
questions.explanation: Series voltages add: 60 * 0.6 = 36 V, at the current of a single cell.

questions.prompt: Compared with a 20% crystalline cell, a 12% thin-film cell needs, for the same power...
questions.explanation: Lower efficiency means more area per watt; area scales as power / (irradiance * efficiency).

questions.prompt: Wiring two identical module strings in parallel changes the array by...
options: removing the need for an inverter
questions.explanation: Parallel connection adds currents at the same voltage; series would add voltages.

lessons.title: Balance of system: inverters, mounting, storage
lessons.grammar_note: The panels are only part of a working system. Everything else needed to deliver usable power - inverter, mounting, wiring, protection, and any batteries - is together called the balance of system.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name the parts of a system beyond the panels and explain what each one does. Warm-up: what device turns the panels' direct current into the alternating current a home or grid uses?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Modules generate direct current, but homes and the grid run on alternating current, so an inverter converts DC to AC, typically at 95 to 98% efficiency, and also runs maximum-power-point tracking to keep the array at its best operating voltage as sunlight changes. Mounting and racking hold the modules at a chosen tilt and orientation; facing the array toward the equator at a tilt near the site latitude captures the most annual energy. Wiring, fuses, and disconnects carry the power safely and let the system be shut down for maintenance. Where power is needed at night or off the grid, batteries store energy, and a charge controller protects them from over-charging and deep discharge. All of these parts together, everything except the modules themselves, are called the balance of system.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Inverter loss: a 5.0 kW array feeding a 96%-efficient inverter delivers 5.0 * 0.96 = 4.8 kW of AC - about 0.2 kW lost as heat. Inverter sizing: designers often size the inverter near the array power; a 5.0 kW array commonly pairs with a 4.5 to 5.0 kW inverter, because the array rarely hits its full rating in real conditions. Battery capacity: to store 6 kWh at a 48 V battery voltage, the charge in amp-hours is energy divided by voltage, 6000 Wh / 48 V = 125 Ah. Usable versus rated: if that battery should only be discharged to 50% to protect its life, you need a rated 2 * 125 = 250 Ah to keep 125 Ah usable.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) A 4.0 kW array feeds a 95% inverter; what AC power comes out? 2) What component tracks the maximum power point? 3) How many amp-hours store 4.8 kWh at 48 V? 4) Why include a charge controller with batteries? 5) Name two things counted as balance of system. Answers: 1) 4.0 * 0.95 = 3.8 kW. 2) The inverter (via its maximum-power-point tracker). 3) 4800 / 48 = 100 Ah. 4) To prevent over-charge and deep discharge that would damage the battery. 5) Any two of: inverter, mounting, wiring, protection devices, batteries, charge controller.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: quoting the array's DC rating as the AC delivered, ignoring the inverter loss. Mistake: sizing a battery to its rated capacity while planning to use all of it, leaving no margin for depth-of-discharge limits. Exit: (a) What does an inverter do? (b) A 5.0 kW array with a 96% inverter delivers how much AC? Answers: converts DC to AC (and tracks the maximum power point); 5.0 * 0.96 = 4.8 kW.

lessons.title: Performance and losses: temperature and shading
lessons.grammar_note: The performance ratio (PR) rolls all real-world losses into one number: PR = actual energy produced / energy expected from the rating and the sunlight. A typical rooftop system runs a PR around 0.75 to 0.85.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Estimate how temperature and shading cut output, and fold all losses into a performance ratio to predict annual yield. Warm-up: when a silicon module heats up above 25 degrees C, does its power rise or fall?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A module's nameplate rating is measured at a cool 25 degrees C, but in the sun cells run much hotter, and silicon loses power as it warms - a typical temperature coefficient is about -0.4% per degree C above 25. Shading hurts more than its share: because cells in a string carry the same current, one shaded cell can throttle the whole string, which is why bypass diodes are built in to route current around shaded groups. Other losses include soiling from dust, mismatch between modules, and resistance in the wiring and inverter. Rather than track each loss separately for a quick estimate, engineers bundle them into a performance ratio and use it to turn sunlight into predicted energy: yearly energy is roughly the array rating in kWp times the site's yearly sun hours in kWh/m^2 times the performance ratio.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Temperature loss: a module rated 300 W runs 30 degrees C above the 25 degrees C reference. With -0.4% per degree C, the loss is 30 * 0.4% = 12%, so output falls to 300 * (1 - 0.12) = 264 W. Annual yield: a 5.0 kWp array at a site receiving 1600 kWh/m^2 per year, with a performance ratio of 0.80, produces about 5.0 * 1600 * 0.80 = 6400 kWh per year. Shading intuition: shading just one cell in a 60-cell series module can, without a bypass diode, cut that module's output by far more than 1/60, because the shaded cell limits the shared string current.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) A 250 W module is 20 degrees C above reference at -0.4% per degree C; what power remains? 2) A 3.0 kWp array sees 1500 kWh/m^2 per year at PR 0.80; estimate the yearly energy. 3) Why does one shaded cell hurt a whole series string? 4) Name one loss besides temperature and shading. 5) A system delivers 6400 kWh where 8000 was expected from sun and rating; what is the PR? Answers: 1) loss = 20 * 0.4% = 8%, so 250 * 0.92 = 230 W. 2) 3.0 * 1500 * 0.80 = 3600 kWh. 3) Series cells share one current, so the weakest cell limits them all. 4) Soiling, module mismatch, or wiring and inverter resistance. 5) PR = 6400 / 8000 = 0.80.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using the 25 degrees C nameplate power for a hot rooftop, which overstates real output. Mistake: treating a small shaded patch as a small loss - without bypass diodes it can cost far more. Exit: (a) A 300 W module loses 0.4% per degree C and runs 25 degrees C hot; what power remains? (b) What single number bundles all real-world losses? Answers: loss 10%, so 270 W; the performance ratio.

lessons.title: Solar thermal versus photovoltaic
lessons.grammar_note: Two different jobs from the same sunlight: photovoltaic makes electricity from photons, while solar thermal makes heat. Match the technology to whether you actually need electricity or hot fluid.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Distinguish solar thermal from photovoltaic systems and pick the right one for a given need. Warm-up: if your goal is simply hot water for a shower, do you need electricity or heat?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Photovoltaic systems, the focus of this course, use the photovoltaic effect to turn light straight into electricity, which is flexible and easy to move but is capped by the single-junction efficiency limits we have seen. Solar thermal systems instead absorb sunlight as heat: a collector warms a fluid that can heat water, warm a building, or, in large concentrated solar power plants, boil water to spin a turbine and generate electricity indirectly. For delivering heat, thermal collectors capture a larger share of the incoming energy than a photovoltaic panel converts to electricity, so if you truly need heat, thermal is often the better match. If you need electricity, or want a system with no moving parts that is simple to install on a roof, photovoltaic usually wins. The two can even coexist as hybrid panels that produce both electricity and heat from the same area.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Choosing by need: a household wanting hot water is served well by a solar thermal collector that might turn 50 to 70% of incoming sunlight into useful heat. The same roof for charging devices and running lights needs a photovoltaic array at roughly 18 to 20% electrical efficiency. Comparing energy: over a day with 5.0 kWh/m^2 of sunlight, a 1 m^2 thermal collector at 60% could deliver about 5.0 * 0.60 = 3.0 kWh of heat, while a 1 m^2 photovoltaic panel at 20% delivers about 5.0 * 0.20 = 1.0 kWh of electricity - more raw energy from thermal, but as lower-grade heat rather than versatile electricity.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which technology makes electricity directly, thermal or photovoltaic? 2) What does a solar thermal collector produce? 3) Over a day of 4.0 kWh/m^2, how much heat does 1 m^2 of a 60% thermal collector give? 4) Over the same day, how much electricity does 1 m^2 of a 20% photovoltaic panel give? 5) What is a hybrid panel? Answers: 1) Photovoltaic. 2) Heat (a warm fluid). 3) 4.0 * 0.60 = 2.4 kWh of heat. 4) 4.0 * 0.20 = 0.8 kWh of electricity. 5) A panel that produces both electricity and heat from the same area.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: comparing thermal and photovoltaic on efficiency alone, when the two deliver different products - heat versus electricity. Mistake: assuming concentrated solar power is photovoltaic; it uses heat to drive a turbine. Exit: (a) Which technology should you pick to heat water directly? (b) Which produces electricity with no moving parts? Answers: solar thermal; photovoltaic.

options: actual energy divided by expected energy
questions.explanation: PR bundles all real losses as actual output divided by the ideal output from rating and sunlight.

questions.explanation: Charge = energy / voltage = 6000 Wh / 48 V = 125 Ah.

questions.explanation: Thermal collectors deliver heat; photovoltaic panels deliver electricity.

lessons.title: Capstone: design a small PV system
lessons.grammar_note: Sizing recipe: array power (kWp) = daily load (kWh) / (peak sun hours * performance ratio). Round the number of panels up, then size the inverter to the array and the battery to the nights you must cover.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Size a small off-grid photovoltaic system end to end: array, number of panels, inverter, and battery. Warm-up: if a home uses 6 kWh a day and each peak sun hour delivers a panel's full rating, why can't you simply divide 6 kWh by the array rating and stop there?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Sizing starts from the daily energy the load needs, then works backward through the sunlight and the losses. The array power in kWp is the daily load divided by the product of peak sun hours and the performance ratio, because both the limited hours of good sun and the real-world losses reduce what a nameplate kilowatt actually delivers. Divide that array power by the power of one panel to get the panel count, and round up. Size the inverter to handle the array power and the largest instantaneous load. For an off-grid system, size the battery to carry the load through the hours or days without sun, and remember to allow for the depth of discharge the battery chemistry permits so you do not plan to drain it fully.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Take a cabin that uses 6.0 kWh per day at a site with 4.5 peak sun hours and a performance ratio of 0.80. Array size: 6.0 / (4.5 * 0.80) = 6.0 / 3.6 = about 1.67 kWp. Panel count: with 400 W panels, 1670 / 400 = 4.2, so round up to 5 panels (2.0 kWp), giving a little headroom. Inverter: pick one rated near 2 kW to match the array and cover normal loads. Battery for one night: store the full 6.0 kWh of daily load; at a 48 V bank that is 6000 / 48 = 125 Ah usable. If the chemistry should only be discharged to 50%, size the rated capacity to 2 * 125 = 250 Ah at 48 V. Cross-check the yield: 2.0 kWp * 4.5 h * 0.80 = 7.2 kWh per day, comfortably above the 6.0 kWh load.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Design for a load of 4.0 kWh/day, 5.0 peak sun hours, PR 0.80, using 400 W panels and a 48 V battery for one night at 50% depth of discharge. 1) Required array power in kWp? 2) Number of 400 W panels (round up)? 3) Daily yield of that rounded array (use its kWp * 5.0 * 0.80)? 4) Usable amp-hours to store 4.0 kWh at 48 V? 5) Rated amp-hours at 50% depth of discharge? Answers: 1) 4.0 / (5.0 * 0.80) = 4.0 / 4.0 = 1.0 kWp. 2) 1000 / 400 = 2.5, round up to 3 panels (1.2 kWp). 3) 1.2 * 5.0 * 0.80 = 4.8 kWh/day, above the 4.0 kWh load. 4) 4000 / 48 = about 83 Ah. 5) 2 * 83 = about 167 Ah.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: dividing the load by peak sun hours alone and skipping the performance ratio, which undersizes the array. Mistake: sizing the battery to its rated capacity while planning to fully discharge it, leaving no depth-of-discharge margin. Exit: (a) Write the array-sizing formula. (b) For a 5.0 kWh/day load, 4.0 peak sun hours, and PR 0.80, what array power do you need? Answers: array kWp = daily load / (peak sun hours * PR); 5.0 / (4.0 * 0.80) = 5.0 / 3.2 = about 1.56 kWp.
